pos: n. (the Pyrenean sovereignty where Jeanne d'Albret established the Reformed religion by law and paid for the Basque New Testament)
etymology: French Béarn, from the Roman Beneharnum; a viscounty held with Navarre, sovereign and not part of the kingdom of France.
biblical_def: Bearn is the small Pyrenean state that was the only sovereignty in the French-speaking world where the Reformed religion was legally established. Jeanne d'Albret, queen of Navarre and sovereign of Bearn, declared for the Reformation in 1560 and from 1563 to 1571 carried it through her territory by ordinance: the mass was suppressed, the churches handed to Reformed ministers, church revenues applied to ministers and schools, and an academy founded at Orthez in 1566. Her most lasting act was linguistic. She commissioned and paid for the translation of the New Testament into Basque, the language of the western part of her lands, and Joanes Leizarraga's version was printed at La Rochelle in 1571, the first substantial book ever printed in Basque and still a monument of the language; she also had the Psalms put into Bearnais. Her son became Henry of Navarre and then king of France, bought Paris with a mass in 1593, and gave the Huguenots the Edict of Nantes in 1598. Bearn's own settlement was overthrown in 1620 when Louis XIII marched in and restored Catholicism. The dictionary enters Bearn because a sovereign princess spent her own revenue on a New Testament for shepherds who spoke a language unrelated to any other in Europe.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a viscounty as the jurisdiction of a viscount; sovereignty as supreme power; an ordinance as a rule established by authority; and an academy as a school of learning.
webster_full: VISCOUNT, n. A degree of nobility next in rank to an earl; formerly an officer who supplied the place of the count.
SOVEREIGNTY, n. Supreme power; supremacy; the possession of the highest power, or of uncontrollable power.
ORDINANCE, n. A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action; a law or statute.
ACADEMY, n. A school or seminary of learning, holding a rank between a university and a common school.
REVENUE, n. The annual rents, profits, interest or issues of any species of property; income.
scriptures: Cretes and Arabians, we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God.

And kings shall be thy nursing fathers, and their queens thy nursing mothers: they shall bow down to thee with their face toward the earth, and lick up the dust of thy feet; and thou shalt know that I am the LORD: for they shall not be ashamed that wait for me.

After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;
The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it.
corruption_summary: Pyrenean sovereignty where Jeanne d'Albret established the Reformed religion by ordinance from 1563 and paid for Leizarraga's Basque New Testament of 1571.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the measuring of a translation by the size of its readership, which would have killed the Basque New Testament before it began. Basque was spoken by a few hundred thousand mountain people, was related to nothing, and had almost no written literature; by every commercial and political argument Jeanne d'Albret should have supplied her Basque subjects with the French Bible and let them manage. She paid for the translation instead, and the men of the valleys could “hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God” (Act 2:11) in a speech no other prince in Europe had ever had printed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the right use of a ruler's revenue, and Scripture gives the picture: “kings shall be thy nursing fathers, and their queens thy nursing mothers” (Isa 49:23). A nursing mother feeds; she does not merely legislate, and the Bearn ordinances were accompanied by a press, a school and a translation. The end for which such labour is spent is the company gathered out of “all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” (Rev 7:9), and of the queen who published it the psalm's word is apt: “great was the company of those that published it” (Psa 68:11).

pos: n. (the Alpine province of Farel's birth, holding the Waldensian valleys that were crusaded against in 1488)
etymology: French Dauphiné, from the title Dauphin borne by its counts and later by the heir to the French throne; the province lies between the Rhone and the Alps.
biblical_def: Dauphine is the Alpine province of France that held Waldensian valleys for three centuries before the Reformation and gave the Reformation one of its first French preachers. In the high valleys west of the Cottian Alps, at Freissinieres, Vallouise, Argentiere and the Val Cluson, communities of Vaudois had kept their own preachers, their own copies of Scripture in the vernacular and their own refusal of the mass since the thirteenth century. In 1487 Innocent VIII proclaimed a crusade against them, and in 1488 the archdeacon of Cremona led troops into the valleys; Vallouise was devastated, the people of the Val Louise suffocated in the cave of Aigue Froide, and Freissinieres held out and survived to send delegates to the Swiss reformers forty years later. Dauphine also produced William Farel, born at Gap about 1489, the man who preached the Reformation into Geneva, Neuchatel and the Vaud and who dragged Calvin into staying there. In the religious wars the province was a Huguenot stronghold under Lesdiguieres. The dictionary enters Dauphine because the Reformation in these valleys was not an importation but a continuation, and the Vaudois of Freissinieres had been holding their ground for two hundred and fifty years when Farel was born.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a crusade as an expedition against infidels; a valley as a hollow between hills; to suffocate as to choke by excluding air; and a delegate as one sent with power to act.
webster_full: CRUSADE, n. A military expedition undertaken by Christians for the recovery of the Holy Land; any expedition undertaken with zeal.
VALLEY, n. A hollow or low tract of land between hills or mountains.
SUFFOCATE, v. To choke or kill by stopping respiration; to extinguish; to smother.
DELEGATE, n. A person appointed and sent by another with powers to transact business as his representative.
CAVERN, n. A deep hollow place in the earth; a cave; a den.

And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people from henceforth even for ever.
But when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another: for verily I say unto you, Ye shall not have gone over the cities of Israel, till the Son of man be come.
corruption_summary: Alpine province of Farel's birth whose Waldensian valleys were crusaded against in 1488, and which became a Huguenot stronghold in the religious wars.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the crusade turned against Christians, which is what Innocent VIII proclaimed in 1487 and what came up the Val Louise in 1488. Men, women and children of these valleys were hunted into a cave at Aigue Froide and killed by smoke and suffocation for holding that the mass is not a sacrifice and that Scripture should be read in a language they knew. They are of the company “slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9), and the dictionary records both the instrument and the authority that ordered it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the lawfulness of flight, which these valleys practised for centuries and which the Lord himself commands: “when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another” (Mat 10:23). Mountains are a mercy to a hunted church, and the figure is Scripture's own, that “As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people” (Psa 125:2). Of men who wandered in deserts and mountains, in dens and caves of the earth, it is written that they were those “Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38).

pos: n. (the southern province of the Cathars and later of the Huguenots, where the Camisards rose in 1702)
etymology: French Languedoc, the langue d'oc, the tongue that says oc for yes, as against the northern langue d'oïl.
biblical_def: Languedoc is the French province most often misdescribed in Protestant histories, because two very different movements were strong there four centuries apart. In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries it was the heartland of the Cathars, whom the dictionary refuses to claim: they were dualists who held matter to be the work of an evil power, denied the incarnation and the resurrection of the body, rejected marriage and the Old Testament, and were destroyed by the Albigensian Crusade from 1209 in a war of appalling cruelty. Their doctrine was not the Reformation's and their persecution was still murder. From the 1550s the same province became the strongest Huguenot country in France: Nimes, Montpellier, Uzes and the Cevennes held Reformed majorities, synods met, academies taught, and the province was a principal party to every religious war. After the Revocation of 1685 the Cevennes rose in 1702 in the revolt of the Camisards, peasant bands with lay prophets who fought the king's armies for two years in the mountains. The dictionary enters Languedoc because the Cathar legend is the commonest false claim made on the Reformation's behalf, and because the Huguenot Languedoc that really was Reformed is remarkable enough without it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dualism as the doctrine of two independent principles; a heresiarch as the leader of a heretical sect; a revocation as the act of annulling; and a prophet as one who foretells future events.
webster_full: DUALISM, n. The doctrine of those who maintain the existence of two distinct and independent principles, one good and the other evil.
HERESIARCH, n. A leader in heresy; the chief of a sect of heretics.
REVOCATION, n. The act of recalling or annulling; the act of repealing or reversing a grant or edict.
PROPHET, n. One that foretells future events; a predicter; a foreteller.
INCARNATION, n. The act of clothing with flesh; the act of assuming flesh, as the Son of God.
scriptures: Hereby know ye the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God:
And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. And the evening and the morning were the sixth day.
For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving:
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
corruption_summary: Southern province of the Cathar dualists and later of the Huguenots, where the Camisards of the Cevennes rose in 1702 after the Revocation.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the claiming of the Cathars as forerunners of the Reformation, which Protestant writers have done since the sixteenth century and which the dictionary rejects. Catharism taught two gods, denied that the Son came in true flesh, and condemned marriage and procreation as the propagation of evil. The apostolic test excludes it absolutely: “Every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God” (1Jo 4:2). That Rome butchered them in the Albigensian Crusade does not make their doctrine ours, and the dictionary holds both facts at once.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the goodness of the created order, which dualism of every age denies. The verdict at the end of the creation week is that God “saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good” (Gen 1:31), and the apostle applies it directly against ascetic prohibitions, that “every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused” (1Ti 4:4). The duty laid on a church that meets a new claim of the Spirit is the one the Camisard prophets also needed: “believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jo 4:1).

pos: n. (the Mediterranean province where the Vaudois villages of Merindol and Cabrieres were massacred by order of a court in 1545)
etymology: French Provence, from Latin provincia, the province, the Roman name for this first Gallic conquest.
biblical_def: Provence is the French province where a high court ordered the destruction of villages and the order was carried out. Waldensian families from the Alpine valleys had settled the Luberon hills through the fifteenth century, clearing waste land at Merindol, Cabrieres and a dozen other villages, and from the 1530s they were in correspondence with the Swiss reformers and had openly joined the Reformation. In November 1540 the Parlement of Aix issued the Arret de Merindol, condemning the inhabitants of Merindol to death and their village to be razed and its woods cut down so that nothing should grow there; it was suspended, revived, and executed in April 1545 by Jean Maynier, baron d'Oppede, president of the Parlement, with troops and papal soldiery. Merindol was destroyed, Cabrieres stormed and its people killed after a surrender on terms, and the usual estimate is some two or three thousand dead across the villages with hundreds sent to the galleys. The dictionary enters Provence because this was not a riot or a war but a judicial sentence on a population, pronounced by a court, and because Francis I ordered an inquiry afterwards that convicted the lesser officers and left Oppede acquitted.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a parlement as a French superior court of justice; an arret as a judgment or decree of a court; to raze as to demolish level with the ground; and a galley as a vessel rowed by slaves.
webster_full: PARLIAMENT, n. In France, before the revolution, a superior court of justice having jurisdiction over a province.
DECREE, n. Judicial decision, or determination of a litigated cause; an edict or law made by a superior.
RAZE, v. To subvert from the foundation; to overthrow; to destroy; to demolish.
GALLEY, n. A low flat-built vessel with one deck, navigated with sails and oars, often rowed by criminals.
AMNESTY, n. An act of oblivion; a general pardon of the offenses of subjects against the government.
scriptures: Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees, and that write grievousness which they have prescribed;
Therefore the law is slacked, and judgment doth never go forth: for the wicked doth compass about the righteous; therefore wrong judgment proceedeth.
Ye who turn judgment to wormwood, and leave off righteousness in the earth,
And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?
corruption_summary: Mediterranean province where the Parlement of Aix condemned Merindol in 1540 and Oppede executed the sentence in April 1545, destroying the Vaudois villages of the Luberon.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the court that writes injustice into law, and Provence holds the Reformation's plainest example. The Arret de Merindol was not a mob's act; it was drafted, registered and pronounced by the superior court of the province, condemning named villages to be razed and their people to death, and it was executed by that court's own president with soldiers. The prophet's woe is addressed precisely to such men: “Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees, and that write grievousness which they have prescribed” (Isa 10:1).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the perversion of judgement is a sin God names and punishes, and that the victims are permitted to ask when. “therefore wrong judgment proceedeth” (Hab 1:4) is the prophet's complaint about his own courts, and Amos says of such judges that they “turn judgment to wormwood” (Amo 5:7). The souls under the altar cry “How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood” (Rev 6:10), and the Luberon dead are among them; Oppede was tried in Paris and acquitted, and the inquiry fell on his subordinates.

pos: n. (the northern province of Rouen, Caen and Dieppe, with a strong Reformed minority and the synod of Alencon of 1637)
etymology: French Normandie, the land of the Northmen, settled by Norse under Rollo from 911.
biblical_def: Normandy is the northern French province where the Reformed church was numerous enough to matter and never numerous enough to be safe. Rouen, Caen, Dieppe and Alencon all held substantial Reformed congregations from the 1550s, drawn from merchants, artisans, printers and a part of the gentry; Rouen was one of the eight places where a national synod of the French churches met, and Caen had a Reformed academy. The province paid in blood for it: Rouen was taken by the Catholic forces in 1562 with a sack, Augustin Marlorat its minister being hanged in the ruins of his own church; the news of the Paris massacre of August 1572 was followed by killings at Rouen, where some hundreds of Protestants were murdered in the prisons in September. The national synod that met at Alencon in 1637 is Normandy's chief theological occasion: it examined Moise Amyraut and Paul Testard of Saumur over the hypothetical universalism they taught, and let them keep their chairs on an undertaking about their manner of teaching. Elie Benoist, pastor at Alencon, wrote after the Revocation the standard history of the Edict of Nantes. The dictionary enters Normandy because Alencon's refusal to condemn Amyraut is where the French Reformed church chose to live with an unsettled doctrine of the extent of the atonement.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a synod as an ecclesiastical council; atonement as expiation and satisfaction; hypothetical as conditional or supposed; and a sack as the pillage of a town.
webster_full: SYNOD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion; an assembly of ministers and elders.
ATONEMENT, n. Expiation; satisfaction or reparation made by giving an equivalent for an injury.
HYPOTHETICAL, a. Including a supposition; conditional; assumed without proof for the purpose of reasoning.
SACK, n. The pillage or plunder of a town or city; the storm and spoil of a place taken by assault.
ACADEMY, n. A school or seminary of learning, holding a rank between a university and a common school.
scriptures: As the Father knoweth me, even so know I the Father: and I lay down my life for the sheep.
Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;
I pray for them: I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me; for they are thine.
He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied: by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities.
corruption_summary: Northern province of Rouen, Caen and Dieppe, where Marlorat was hanged in 1562 and the synod of Alencon in 1637 declined to condemn Amyraut.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the universal intention of the atonement, which Amyraut taught at Saumur as a decree to save all men on condition of faith, with the effectual decree following; and the dictionary holds that this makes the Son's work wider than the Father's election and the Spirit's application, which Scripture does not. The Lord states the extent himself in the same breath as the act: “I lay down my life for the sheep” (Joh 10:15), and the husband's pattern is that “Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it” (Eph 5:25). Alencon in 1637 did not condemn it, and the Helvetic Consensus had to deal with it thirty-eight years later.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the definite success of the atonement, which is what makes it good news to anybody. The high priestly prayer is deliberately bounded: “I pray not for the world, but for them which thou hast given me” (Joh 17:9). And the servant's satisfaction is guaranteed, not offered: “He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied” (Isa 53:11). The dictionary records that Amyraut was a serious and devout man and that Normandy's synod acted charitably toward him, and that the charity cost the French church a settled doctrine.

pos: n. (the Celtic-speaking western province the Reformation scarcely reached, and which got its New Testament in Breton in 1827)
etymology: French Bretagne, the land of the Britons who crossed from Britain in the fifth and sixth centuries; Breton Breizh.
biblical_def: Brittany is the French province where the Reformation failed most completely, and the reason is mostly linguistic. The duchy, united to France only in 1532, was Celtic-speaking across its western half; Breton is a British tongue, cousin to Welsh and Cornish, and the peasantry of Lower Brittany spoke no French. The Reformation in France was carried by French books, French psalters and French-speaking preachers out of Geneva, and it reached the French-speaking towns of the east, Nantes and Rennes, in small numbers and the Breton-speaking west hardly at all; no Reformed body ever attempted a Breton Bible. Rome did the vernacular work instead. Michel Le Nobletz from 1610 and Julien Maunoir from 1640 ran missions through Lower Brittany preaching in Breton, with Breton catechisms, Breton hymns and painted boards to teach the illiterate, and Maunoir published a Breton grammar and dictionary; the Breton countryside was catechised in its own language by Jesuits while the Reformed preached French in the towns. A Breton New Testament came only in 1827, from Jean-Francois Le Gonidec, and the whole Bible in 1866. The dictionary enters Brittany because the Reformation's own first principle was here applied by its opponents, and that is a judgement we should be willing to record.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Celtic as pertaining to the primitive inhabitants of the south and west of Europe; a catechism as instruction by question and answer; a grammar as the art of writing a language correctly; and a mission as a sending to preach.
webster_full: CELTIC, a. Pertaining to the primitive inhabitants of the south and west of Europe, or to the early inhabitants of Italy, Gaul, Spain and Britain.
CATECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
GRAMMAR, n. The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety; a system of general principles of a language.
MISSION, n. A sending; persons sent with commission, as to preach the gospel; a station of missionaries.
DIALECT, n. The form or idiom of a language peculiar to a province, or to a kingdom or state.
scriptures: So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.
And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?
And the lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely: for the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light.
And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?
corruption_summary: Celtic-speaking western province the Reformation scarcely entered, catechised in Breton by Le Nobletz and Maunoir from 1610, and given a Breton New Testament only in 1827.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is ours, and it is the failure to translate. The Reformed churches of France held, correctly, that a man must hear the word in his own tongue, and then preached French at Breton speakers for two hundred and fifty years without attempting a Breton Scripture. The apostle's question stands against us in this province: “how shall it be known what is spoken?” (1Co 14:9). The dictionary declines the excuse that the Reformed in Brittany were too few, since the Breton missions of the next century were run by two priests and some painted boards.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a true principle is worth nothing until it is acted on, and that an opponent who acts on it has the better of the argument. The Lord's own comment on worldly diligence applies without flattery to Maunoir's Breton grammar: “the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light” (Luk 16:8). The Pentecostal standard is unchanged, that men hear “in our own tongue, wherein we were born” (Act 2:8), and the warning about looking at a brother's fault is in place here: “why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye” (Mat 7:3).

“the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light” (Luk 16:8) — Maunoir's Breton grammar and catechisms.
“in our own tongue, wherein we were born” (Act 2:8) — a Breton New Testament only in 1827.

pos: n. (the northern province that produced Calvin and Lefevre d'Etaples, and was then held hard for Rome)
etymology: French Picardie, probably from picard, a pikeman, or from a dialect word; the province lies between the Somme and the Oise.
biblical_def: Picardy is the French province that gave the Reformation two of its most important Frenchmen and kept almost none of their work. Jacques Lefevre d'Etaples, born at Etaples on the Picard coast about 1455, was the humanist who published commentaries on the Psalms and on Paul before Luther posted anything, taught justification by faith in Paris, translated the whole Bible into French between 1523 and 1530, and led the circle at Meaux under Bishop Brionnet that was France's first evangelical experiment. John Calvin was born at Noyon in Picardy in 1509, the son of a cathedral notary, and held Picard benefices as a boy before he left for Paris, Orleans and finally Basel and Geneva. Picardy was also the route of every northern army and was held firmly for the crown and the old religion; its evangelical groups, numerous in the 1520s and 1530s among weavers and small traders, were broken up by the Parlement of Paris, and the province had no Huguenot stronghold of its own. The dictionary enters Picardy because the Reformation's greatest French theologian and its first French translator were both Picards who did their work somewhere else, which is the ordinary history of exiles.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a benefice as an ecclesiastical living; a notary as a public officer who attests deeds; a humanist as one versed in the knowledge of human nature and letters; and exile as banishment.
webster_full: BENEFICE, n. In the church, an ecclesiastical living; a church endowed with a revenue for the maintenance of divine service.
NOTARY, n. An officer authorized to attest contracts or writings of any kind, to give them the evidence of authenticity.
HUMANIST, n. One versed in the knowledge of human nature; a professor of grammar and rhetoric; a philologist.
EXILE, n. One who is banished from his own country, or who abandons it for his own safety.
WEAVER, n. One whose occupation is to weave; one who makes cloth.
scriptures: By faith he sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, the heirs with him of the same promise:
And said unto him, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and come into the land which I shall shew thee.
Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee:

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
corruption_summary: Northern province, birthplace of Lefevre d'Etaples and of Calvin at Noyon in 1509, whose own evangelical groups were broken up and which kept no Huguenot stronghold.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the expectation that a man's labour will be spent where he was born. Lefevre translated the French Bible and died at Nerac under Marguerite of Navarre's protection; Calvin wrote the Institutes at Basel and governed a church at Geneva; neither had a congregation in Picardy, and the weavers of Amiens and Noyon who first read their books were dispersed or burned. The call to Abraham is the pattern: “Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and come into the land which I shall shew thee” (Act 7:3).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the people of God are sojourners by vocation, not by accident. Abraham “sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles” (Heb 11:9), and the whole company of them died “not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off” (Heb 11:13). Calvin's own first command was Abraham's: “Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house” (Gen 12:1), and Picardy is the country he got out of.

roots_lines: Greek paroikeo (G3939) — to dwell beside, to sojourn; “sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country”, Hebrews 11:9.
Greek skene (G4633) — a tent, a tabernacle; “dwelling in tabernacles”, Hebrews 11:9.

Hebrew yalak (H3212) — to go, to walk, to depart; “Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house”, Genesis 12:1.

“sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country” (Heb 11:9) — Lefevre dying under protection at Nerac.
“but having seen them afar off” (Heb 11:13) — weavers of Amiens dispersed by the Parlement of Paris.

pos: n. (the south-western province of the Albret lands and the Gascon Huguenot nobility, and of Clairac and Nerac)
etymology: French Gascogne, from Vasconia, the land of the Vascones or Basques; the province lies between the Garonne and the Pyrenees.
biblical_def: Gascony is the south-western country whose nobility made the Huguenot cause a military power. A land of small towns, vineyards and a numerous and poor gentry with a strong tradition of arms, it fell largely within the Albret inheritance, so that when Jeanne d'Albret declared for the Reformation her Gascon vassals followed; Nerac became a Reformed court and Clairac, Caumont and a string of bastide towns held Reformed garrisons. Its Protestant gentlemen supplied much of the cavalry of the religious wars, and the king who ended those wars, Henry of Navarre, was raised among them at Nerac and Pau. That military character was the province's strength and its spiritual danger: a cause carried by gentlemen with horses and quarrels tends to be defended as a party and a privilege, and when Henry conformed to Rome in 1593 to secure Paris, a great part of the Gascon nobility followed him into the Catholic church within a generation, their estates being easier to keep that way. The dictionary enters Gascony because the Reformation there was genuinely held and largely held by a class, and when the class found its interest lay elsewhere the province went with it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a vassal as one who holds land of a superior; a bastide as a fortified town; cavalry as horsemen in military service; and to conform as to comply with or yield obedience.
webster_full: VASSAL, n. A feudatory; a tenant; one who holds land of a superior and vows fidelity and homage to him.
FORTRESS, n. A fortified place; a large and permanent fortification for the defense of a country.
CAVALRY, n. A body of troops whose members serve on horseback; horsemen armed for war.
CONFORM, v. To comply with or yield obedience to; to make like in manners or opinions.
GENTRY, n. People of education and good breeding; the class between the nobility and the yeomanry.
scriptures: No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
And when he heard this, he was very sorrowful: for he was very rich.
But when the young man heard that saying, he went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions.
But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.
corruption_summary: South-western province of the Albret lands whose Huguenot nobility supplied the cause its cavalry, and largely followed Henry of Navarre back to Rome after 1593.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the religion held as a class interest, which is secure exactly as long as the interest runs with it. The Gascon gentry were Reformed because their overlords were and because the cause gave them standing, commands and a grievance against the crown; when the Edict of Nantes gave them security and the court gave their sons careers, the estates and the pensions argued the other way, and a great many conformed. The Lord's word is not a figure of speech: “No man can serve two masters” (Mat 6:24).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that property is the commonest obstacle to discipleship in Scripture's own examples. The young ruler “went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions” (Mat 19:22), and of the same man Luke records that “when he heard this, he was very sorrowful: for he was very rich” (Luk 18:23). The apostolic warning follows the Gascon pattern exactly, that “they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare” (1Ti 6:9). The dictionary records that many Gascon families did not conform and lost the estates instead.
roots_summary: Greek douleuo (G1398), to serve as a slave; Greek ktema (G2933), a possession; Greek pagis (G3803), a snare.
roots_lines: Greek douleuo (G1398) — to serve as a bondman; “No man can serve two masters”, Matthew 6:24.
Greek mammon (G3126) — riches, wealth personified; “Ye cannot serve God and mammon”, Matthew 6:24.
Greek ktema (G2933) — a possession, an estate; “for he had great possessions”, Matthew 19:22.
Greek perilupos (G4036) — very sorrowful, deeply grieved; “he was very sorrowful: for he was very rich”, Luke 18:23.
Greek pagis (G3803) — a trap, a snare; “fall into temptation and a snare”, 1 Timothy 6:9.
usage: “No man can serve two masters” (Mat 6:24) — a Reformed gentry whose interest changed after 1593.
“for he had great possessions” (Mat 19:22) — estates easier to keep in the Catholic church.
“they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare” (1Ti 6:9) — Nerac a Reformed court and Clairac a garrison.

pos: n. (the Loire city where Calvin studied law, and which was the Huguenot capital in the first religious war)
etymology: French Orléans, from Latin Aurelianum, named for the emperor Aurelian; the city stands at the northern bend of the Loire.
biblical_def: Orleans is the Loire city that trained Calvin as a lawyer and then served the Huguenots as a capital. Its university was the chief law faculty of France and full of German and other foreign students, who enjoyed privileges and a certain protection; Calvin was sent there by his father about 1528 to read law under Pierre de l'Estoile, learned the method of close textual argument that marks everything he afterwards wrote, took his licence, and formed friendships with men already reading Luther. The city's Reformed congregation became one of the largest in France, and in 1562, at the opening of the first religious war, Conde made Orleans the Huguenot headquarters: the churches were taken, a mint struck coin, the national synod met there in 1562, and Theodore Beza was in attendance on the prince. It was outside Orleans in February 1563 that Francis, duke of Guise, was shot by Poltrot de Mere, a Protestant gentleman, and died, an assassination the Reformed leadership disclaimed and which the dictionary names as murder. The city was surrendered under the Peace of Amboise. The dictionary enters Orleans because Calvin's legal training is the key to his exegesis, and because the Huguenot capital is where the cause acquired a mint, an army and an assassin.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines jurisprudence as the science of law; exegesis as exposition or explanation; a mint as a place where money is coined; and assassination as the killing of a person by surprise.
webster_full: JURISPRUDENCE, n. The science of law; the knowledge of the laws, customs and rights of men necessary for the due administration of justice.
EXEGESIS, n. Exposition; explanation; interpretation, particularly of the Scriptures.
MINT, n. The place where money is coined by public authority.
ASSASSINATION, n. The act of killing or murdering by surprise or secret assault.
LICENCE, n. Authority or liberty given to do any act; a certificate giving permission to practise a profession.
scriptures: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
corruption_summary: Loire city whose law faculty trained Calvin from 1528, and which Conde made the Huguenot capital in 1562, where Guise was assassinated in February 1563.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is political assassination done in the cause's name, and the dictionary puts it plainly: Poltrot de Mere shot the duke of Guise from cover and was a Protestant gentleman, and the commandment is not suspended by a civil war. “Thou shalt not kill” (Exo 20:13) covers a tyrant's general as it covers a village. Coligny was accused of complicity and denied it under oath, and the dictionary records both the accusation and the denial; ten years later the Guise family had him murdered in Paris, and that was murder too.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that vengeance is reserved, and reserved precisely so that the aggrieved do not take it: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord” (Rom 12:19). Orleans' better legacy is intellectual, and the dictionary values it highly: the discipline of reading a text closely for what it actually says, which Calvin learned in a law school, is what “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15) requires, and it produced the commentaries. The Berean habit of men who “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11) is the same virtue in a congregation.
roots_summary: Greek orthotomeo (G3718), to cut straight; Hebrew ratsach (H7523), to murder; Greek ekdikesis (G1557), vengeance.
roots_lines: Greek orthotomeo (G3718) — to cut straight, to handle rightly; “rightly dividing the word of truth”, 2 Timothy 2:15.
Greek anakrino (G350) — to examine, to sift by inquiry; “searched the scriptures daily”, Acts 17:11.
Hebrew ratsach (H7523) — to murder, to slay unlawfully; “Thou shalt not kill”, Exodus 20:13.
Greek ekdikesis (G1557) — vengeance, the execution of right; “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord”, Romans 12:19.
Greek antapodidomi (G467) — to repay, to recompense; “I will repay, saith the Lord”, Romans 12:19.
usage: “Thou shalt not kill” (Exo 20:13) — Guise shot outside Orleans, February 1563.
“rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15) — a law faculty that taught Calvin close reading.
“Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord” (Rom 12:19) — a Huguenot capital with a mint and an army.

pos: n. (the western province of the first Reformed congregations in France, and the home country of Andre Rivet)
etymology: French Poitou, from the Pictones, the Gallic people of the region; the province lies between the Loire and the Charente.
biblical_def: Poitou is the western French province where the earliest Reformed congregations in the kingdom were gathered. Calvin, having left Paris in 1534, spent time in Poitiers and the country round it, and the tradition of the French churches is that the first Reformed communion in France was celebrated with a small company in a cave or grotto near Croutelle outside the city, which is the sort of beginning the Reformation in France had everywhere: a handful of people, a borrowed room or a hole in a hillside, and the Supper taken in the words of Scripture. From that nucleus Poitou became one of the most thoroughly Reformed provinces in France, with a numerous Protestant gentry, strong congregations at Niort, Saint-Maixent, Chatellerault and Poitiers, and a share in every synod. It produced Andre Rivet of Saint-Maixent, who pastored at Thouars, went to Leiden in 1620 as professor, and became one of the great Reformed scholastics and the tutor of the prince of Orange. The Revocation of 1685 fell on Poitou with particular severity, the dragonnades of billeted soldiers having been pioneered there by the intendant Marillac in 1681. The dictionary enters Poitou because the French Reformation began in small secret companies, and this is the province that remembers it best.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a grotto as a natural cave; a dragonnade as the persecution of Protestants by dragoons; an intendant as one who has the charge of a province; and a nucleus as a kernel or central mass.
webster_full: GROTTO, n. A large cave or den; a natural cave or rent in the earth; a place of shade or retreat.
DRAGOON, n. A soldier or trooper who serves on horseback or on foot, as occasion requires.
INTENDANT, n. One who has the charge, oversight, care or direction of some office or employment.
NUCLEUS, n. A kernel; any body about which matter is collected; the central mass.
BILLET, v. To quarter soldiers in private houses by direction or warrant.
scriptures: For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them.
And when he had considered the thing, he came to the house of Mary the mother of John, whose surname was Mark; where many were gathered together praying.
Likewise greet the church that is in their house. Salute my wellbeloved Epaenetus, who is the firstfruits of Achaia unto Christ.
And upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread, Paul preached unto them, ready to depart on the morrow; and continued his speech until midnight.
corruption_summary: Western province where the first Reformed congregations in France were gathered about Poitiers in 1534, and home of Andre Rivet of Saint-Maixent.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the dragonnade, the billeting of soldiers in Protestant houses with licence to behave as they pleased until the household abjured, which was tried in Poitou by the intendant Marillac in 1681 and then used across France. It was designed to produce conversions without producing martyrs, and it worked: tens of thousands signed. The dictionary names it as persecution of a particularly cowardly kind, and declines to count the signatures as changes of mind.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a church needs no building and no numbers to be a church. “For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Mat 18:20) is the charter of a company in a cave at Croutelle, and the apostolic churches met the same way, in Mary's house where “many were gathered together praying” (Act 12:12) and in the house Paul greets as “the church that is in their house” (Rom 16:5). The order of such a meeting is given too, that “upon the first day of the week” (Act 20:7) the disciples came together to break bread.
roots_summary: Greek sunago (G4863), to gather together; Greek ekklesia (G1577), the assembly; Greek oikos (G3624), a house.
roots_lines: Greek sunago (G4863) — to gather together, to assemble; “where two or three are gathered together in my name”, Matthew 18:20.
Greek onoma (G3686) — a name; “gathered together in my name”, Matthew 18:20.
Greek proseuchomai (G4336) — to pray; “where many were gathered together praying”, Acts 12:12.
Greek ekklesia (G1577) — an assembly called out, the church; “the church that is in their house”, Romans 16:5.
Greek klao (G2806) — to break, as bread; “the disciples came together to break bread”, Acts 20:7.
usage: “where two or three are gathered together in my name” (Mat 18:20) — the first Reformed communion in France, near Croutelle.
“the church that is in their house” (Rom 16:5) — congregations at Niort, Saint-Maixent and Chatellerault.
“the disciples came together to break bread” (Act 20:7) — the dragonnades pioneered in this province in 1681.
